did_you_know.text: Did you know? In the same prophecy, Hosea addresses three leadership groups—the priests, the house of Israel, and the royal house—and holds them responsible because they have been a “snare” and a “net” for the people.
Did you know? The prophet emphasizes that the LORD knows Ephraim and Israel, so their sin is not hidden from him; Ephraim has prostituted itself, and Israel has defiled itself.
Did you know? According to the verse, Israel’s deeds do not lead them to return to their God because a “spirit of prostitution” is within them, and they do not know the LORD.
Did you know? Israel’s pride does not protect it: it will testify against them, and Israel, Ephraim, and even Judah will stumble because of their guilt.
Did you know? Israel and Judah try to seek the LORD with flocks and herds, but the sacrifices do them no good, and the verse says, “They will not find him.”
Did you know? Israel’s unfaithfulness to the LORD is also described as giving birth to “foreign children,” and afterward comes the warning that a month will devour their portions.
Did you know? The ram’s horn and trumpet serve as alarm signals here: the blast is heard in Gibeah and Ramah, and the call is also directed to Beth-aven and Benjamin.
Did you know? The leaders of Judah are compared to “those who move boundary markers,” meaning people who shift property boundaries, and the prophet announces that anger will be poured out on them.
Did you know? The punishment is described through two images of slow, ongoing damage: the LORD will be like a moth to Ephraim and like rot to the house of Judah.
Did you know? When Ephraim and Judah recognize their distress, they turn to Assyria and to King Jareb, but the prophet declares that Assyria will not be able to heal them.
Did you know? At the end of the chapter, the LORD is described as returning to his place until Israel acknowledges its guilt and seeks his presence; in their distress, they will earnestly seek him.
